slides.title: Moving objects acquire a filial preference
body: **Filial imprinting** is the learning through which a newly hatched bird develops a preference for a familiar social target. Domestic chicks can acquire this preference for an artificial moving object, even though the object supplies neither milk nor parental care.

Yamaguchi and colleagues trained chicks with moving yellow LEGO blocks. A later choice test presented the familiar yellow object and a novel red object. Greater approach to the familiar target measured the learned visual preference independently of the original training encounter.

The target’s movement recruits following behavior, while its visible features distinguish it from alternatives. Early experience therefore gives an otherwise arbitrary object a selective behavioral role: chicks approach that particular object rather than every available moving stimulus.

slides.title: Artificial targets isolate imprinting cues
body: An artificial caregiver allows the visual identity of an attachment target to be changed while its movement remains controlled. In the chick experiments, yellow and red LEGO objects provided distinguishable visual stimuli rather than two living adults with different calls or behavior.

Training and preference testing were separate procedures. Chicks encountered the training object for 1 hour and subsequently chose between familiar and unfamiliar targets. A preference required discrimination between the objects, whereas activity during training measured approach to a moving stimulus.

The two measurements separate participation in the encounter from what is learned about the target. Following creates repeated exposure to visual features, and the later choice expresses a memory of those features. Artificial targets thus isolate a sensory component of filial attachment.

slides.title: Sensitive periods constrain early attachment
body: A **sensitive period** is a developmental interval during which a particular experience readily changes later behavior. Newly hatched chicks learn a filial preference during their first few days, whereas older untrained chicks ordinarily acquire little preference under the same training conditions.

Brain thyroid hormones change around hatching. **Thyroxine**, or T4, is a circulating precursor; **triiodothyronine**, or T3, is its more active product. Brain T3 declines over the first several days, linking the timing of early learning to a changing hormonal environment.

This developmental change concerns responsiveness to experience rather than the visual identity of the caregiver. The familiar object still supplies the information that is learned. Hormonal state changes whether exposure to that information can establish a new filial preference.

slides.title: Imprinting increases brain Dio2 expression
body: **Dio2**, type 2 iodothyronine deiodinase, is an enzyme that converts T4 into T3 by removing an iodine atom. Its expression increased in the chick brain after imprinting training, coupling sensory experience to local production of an active hormone.

Trained chicks had greater Dio2 expression than chicks kept in darkness or exposed to light without imprinting. The comparison separates exposure to illumination from experience with the moving target. Dio2 labeling included the **intermediate medial mesopallium**, or IMM, a forebrain region involved in visual imprinting.

Learning-related hormone production therefore occurs within the developing brain. Circulating precursor can be converted where learning is occurring, and the resulting T3 changes the tissue’s capacity to acquire a preference. Experience and developmental state interact through this local biochemical step.

slides.title: Brain capillaries convert T4 into active T3
body: Brain capillaries contain endothelial cells, the cells forming the vessel wall. Dio2 labeling colocalized with a capillary marker in these cells. The enzyme’s position provides a route by which blood-borne T4 can be converted into T3 near brain tissue.

The investigators followed radioactively labeled T4 and detected labeled T3 in the brain. **Iopanoic acid**, an inhibitor of deiodination, reduced this conversion. Blocking conversion also impaired imprinting, connecting hormone metabolism with acquisition of the familiar-object preference.

After training, brain T3 was about 1.7 times higher than in control conditions, while serum T3 did not increase comparably. Local conversion changes the hormonal signal available to brain cells without requiring an equivalent rise throughout the circulation.

slides.title: T3 restores learning within an age boundary
body: T3 administered 30 minutes before training restored filial imprinting in previously untrained chicks on days 4–6. Untreated chicks of these ages normally learned little under the same conditions. Hormone treatment extended the ages at which the moving object could establish a preference.

The same acute treatment was ineffective on days 8–10. This age boundary means that declining T3 is one component of the closing sensitive period, while later developmental changes further restrict responsiveness to a single hormone exposure.

Timing relative to the experience also mattered. Giving T3 before training promoted learning; administering it after training, before preference testing, did not produce the same rescue. Its effective action concerns acquisition during the encounter rather than simply increasing approach during the choice test.

slides.title: Local thyroid action changes learning capacity
body: T3 acts locally in the IMM to promote imprinting. Blocking thyroid-hormone receptors or hormone transport there prevented rescue of learning in older chicks. A **receptor** is a cellular protein that binds a signal and changes the cell’s response to it.

The PI3K inhibitor wortmannin also blocked the T3 effect. **PI3K**, phosphoinositide 3-kinase, participates in intracellular signaling. The authors proposed a hypothesis in which rapid thyroid signaling engages this pathway to change the IMM’s responsiveness during the training encounter.

T4 rescue additionally required conversion into T3: iopanoic acid blocked the effect of the precursor. Transport, conversion and receptor-dependent signaling are therefore separable steps connecting hormone availability to the neural processes that establish a selective visual preference.

slides.title: Early hormone exposure primes later learning
body: **Priming** is a lasting change that makes a later learning experience more effective. Chicks imprinted on day 1 could acquire another preference on day 4, after the normal sensitive period, while retaining the earlier preference.

T3 exposure on day 1 also permitted later imprinting even when the chicks had received no early visual training. Early hormone exposure therefore altered future learning capacity rather than merely preserving a memory of the first target.

The history of exposure mattered more than age alone. Acute T3 on day 8 was ineffective, but prior T3 treatment permitted learning at that later age. A transient developmental signal can leave a longer-lasting change in the brain’s capacity to learn from subsequent social experience.

slides.title: Imprinting recruits connected forebrain regions
body: The IMM participates in acquiring a familiar-object preference, but imprinting also involves the **intermediate hyperpallium apicale**, or IMHA, another forebrain region. Aoki and colleagues investigated the connection between these regions using anatomical tracing and localized lesions.

An **anterograde tracer** labels projections extending away from an injection site. After tracer injection into IMM, labeled axons appeared in IMHA. A **retrograde tracer** placed in IMHA labeled neuronal cell bodies in IMM, identifying neurons whose projections reach the injected region.

These complementary directions connect the same anatomical sites. The behavioral experiments then assigned different functions to those sites: early IMM signaling promotes learning, while an intact downstream IMHA is required for acquisition and later expression of the preference.

slides.title: Tracers identify an IMM-to-IMHA pathway
body: An axon is the projection through which a neuron transmits signals to other cells. Viral labeling in IMM marked axonal fibers within IMHA, providing anatomical evidence for communication between the two imprinting-related forebrain regions.

Retrograde cholera-toxin labeling from IMHA identified IMM neurons projecting toward it. Wheat-germ agglutinin, a tracer that can pass between connected cells, provided an additional measure of connectivity. Labeling in IMHA overlapped **NeuN**, a marker used to identify neurons.

Projection labeling and neuronal labeling answer complementary anatomical questions: which region sends fibers to the target, and whether labeled target cells are neurons. Together they support a pathway through which changes initiated in IMM can influence downstream neuronal processing in IMHA.

slides.title: IMHA lesions disrupt preference acquisition
body: Chicks with IMHA lesions approached the moving training object but acquired a much weaker preference for it. Their retained approach activity separates a failure to learn target identity from a general loss of movement or willingness to follow.

The lesions were made with **ibotenic acid**, a compound that damages neurons near the injection site. Training consisted of two 1-hour encounters with a rotating yellow LEGO object. The choice test contrasted that object with a similarly shaped red object.

Lesions in a neighboring control region spared preference acquisition. Histological examination located the damaged tissue and checked surrounding visual-input regions. The regional comparison connects the acquisition deficit to IMHA involvement in learning the visual identity of the attachment target.

slides.title: T3 rescue requires an intact downstream region
body: T3 given before training can restore imprinting in 4-day-old chicks. When IMHA was lesioned, the same systemic hormone treatment failed to restore a familiar-object preference. Hormone availability therefore depends on an intact neural pathway to change behavior.

The trained object was a moving yellow LEGO target, and the subsequent test measured time spent approaching yellow versus red targets. Control chicks receiving T3 developed a preference; IMHA-lesioned chicks remained poor at selecting the familiar object.

The pharmacological and anatomical manipulations affect different levels of the process. T3 changes learning capacity, while IMHA provides neural processing required to use that capacity. Increasing a permissive signal does not replace the neurons that support the resulting memory-guided choice.

slides.title: Local T3 actions differ across forebrain regions
body: T3 delivered directly into IMM restored imprinting in older chicks, whereas delivery into IMHA did not. The connected regions are therefore not interchangeable sites of thyroid action, despite both participating in the learned preference.

IMHA lesions also prevented rescue when T3 was injected into IMM. Local hormone action in the upstream region required the downstream region to remain intact. This combination links the effective site of hormone treatment to a second region needed for the behavioral outcome.

The authors proposed a hypothesis in which thyroid-dependent changes in IMM enable learning-related signals to reach IMHA. The results assign hormone sensitivity to IMM and behavioral dependence to IMHA, combining molecular modulation with the organization of the imprinting pathway.

slides.title: Post-training lesions disrupt later retrieval
body: IMHA remained necessary after a preference had already been learned. Chicks trained on day 1 were tested on day 2, lesioned after that test, and tested again on day 3. IMHA lesions reduced their subsequent familiar-object preference.

IMM lesions at this later stage spared the preference. The timing distinguishes regions required early in learning from those required once experience has already changed behavior. A region can contribute to acquisition without remaining necessary for every later retrieval.

The authors proposed that IMHA might support storage of the learned preference. Lesion-induced loss of expression establishes its involvement in later retrieval, while storage is the proposed interpretation. Developmental learning therefore changes which parts of the connected pathway remain essential for behavior.

slides.title: First social exposure changes robot attachment
body: Japanese quail chicks formed different social attachments depending on their first partner. On day 1, one group encountered another chick and a second group encountered a mobile robot. From day 2 onward, both groups lived in triads containing two chicks and one robot.

The robot carried a simplified bird-head decoy and moved through the rearing arena. Chicks first exposed to it later coordinated their behavior more strongly with the robot. Chicks first exposed to another chick coordinated more strongly with their living companion.

The identical later group composition makes the first encounter biologically significant. Subsequent access to both partners did not immediately erase the earlier difference. Early social experience selected which available partner acquired the strongest control over following and coordinated activity.

slides.title: Robots provide social cues without providing care
body: A mobile robot can supply movement, a visible head and recorded calls without performing all functions of a parent. Jolly and colleagues used an e-puck robot with a bird-head decoy in an arena containing separate heating and feeding zones.

The robot moved at about 0.1 m/s, a speed compatible with chick following. Its autonomous program alternated exploration with pauses near heating and food. Food and warmth came from the arena rather than from the robot itself.

This separation exposes the cues supporting social attraction while maintaining the chicks’ physical needs independently. Practical interaction also required safe locomotion: the study reported a chick becoming trapped by the robot. Social responsiveness and safe operation are distinct requirements for an artificial companion.

slides.title: Chicks synchronize feeding with a robot
body: **Behavioral synchronization** occurs when partners perform an activity together rather than independently. The investigators recorded which arena zones chicks and robots occupied at 2-minute intervals, then quantified overlap in the feeding zone.

Robot-first chicks had stronger chick–robot feeding synchronization than chick-first animals on days 2–4. The groups nevertheless allocated broadly similar amounts of time to feeding and resting. The difference concerned which partner accompanied an activity rather than simply how much food-directed activity occurred.

The synchronization measure accounted for occupancy of the feeding zone. Its chance expectation depended on the robot’s own feeding-zone time, so simultaneous presence was interpreted relative to opportunity. Early attachment altered coordination with a particular partner during ordinary daily behavior.

body: Distress calls increased when a quail chick lost its preferred social companion. On day 5, the researchers removed partners in a fixed sequence, counting calls during six 4-minute phases of separation and reunion.

body: Returning the robot after isolation greatly reduced calling in robot-first chicks. slides.title: Contact comfort organizes surrogate attachment
body: Infant rhesus monkeys preferred prolonged contact with a soft surrogate over a wire surrogate. **Contact comfort** describes the soothing tactile contact obtained by clinging to the cloth-covered surface. Harlow separated this feature from the provision of milk.

The cloth surrogate had a covered, padded body that supported grasping and close contact. The wire surrogate also supported the infant and could supply milk. Each infant had access to both objects, making the preferred surface a choice within the same rearing environment.

Clinging concentrated on the cloth surrogate even when the wire surrogate supplied food. Attachment behavior therefore depended strongly on the properties of bodily contact. A substitute caregiver acquired a preferred role through sensory comfort as well as through the infant’s repeated experience with it.

slides.title: Milk source does not determine contact preference
body: Harlow counterbalanced feeding across surrogate types: some infants received milk from the cloth surrogate and others from the wire surrogate. This arrangement tested whether preference followed food delivery or the tactile properties of the object.

Infants in both conditions spent far more time on cloth. Wire-fed infants approached the wire surrogate to obtain milk but returned to cloth for prolonged contact. Feeding and attachment-directed contact could therefore be assigned to different objects within the same environment.

The behavioral separation explains why an object that supplies calories need not become the principal source of comfort. The infant’s actions depended on the immediate need: food directed brief visits to the nipple, while soft bodily contact maintained a much longer relationship with the cloth surrogate.

slides.title: Cloth preference persists during development
body: The preference for cloth continued over many weeks rather than disappearing after the earliest feeding encounters. Harlow followed surrogate contact across roughly 165 days, including infants receiving milk from either surrogate type.

Cloth contact remained high under both feeding arrangements, while contact with wire remained comparatively low. Repeated access to the milk source therefore failed to transfer the prolonged-contact preference from the cloth object to the wire object.

Additional infants reared with only one surrogate had comparable milk intake and weight gain across surrogate types. Adequate feeding was compatible with very different contact experiences. Nutritional support and tactile attachment are distinct dimensions of substitute caregiving, each expressed through different patterns of infant behavior.

slides.title: Threat directs infants toward the cloth surrogate
body: A frightening moving toy elicited approach to the cloth surrogate. The infant clung to its familiar soft surface rather than treating the milk-providing wire object as an equivalent refuge. The preferred caregiver regulated behavior during an acute challenge.

Attachment was therefore expressed in more than resting contact time. A threat reorganized the infant’s behavior toward rapid proximity and clinging to the familiar surrogate. The same object that supported prolonged everyday contact also became the target of defensive approach when the environment changed.

slides.title: Surrogate access changes exploration
body: Infants placed in an unfamiliar room initially clung to the cloth surrogate and then explored nearby objects, returning periodically to contact it. The familiar object functioned as a base from which the infant could engage with an otherwise unfamiliar environment.

When the surrogate was absent, infants more often crouched, froze or vocalized rather than exploring. The open-field test lasted 3 minutes, allowing a direct comparison of behavior with and without access to the familiar attachment object.

Familiarity also affected behavior when the surrogate was visible behind a barrier. Visual access reduced distress even when physical contact was prevented, although direct contact was more effective. Tactile access and recognition of the familiar caregiver both contributed to regulation of exploration.

slides.title: Older monkeys can form new surrogate preferences
body: Monkeys first given access to cloth and wire surrogates at about 250 days initially avoided the unfamiliar objects. Fear diminished with continued exposure, and the animals developed a strong preference for the cloth surrogate.

Within approximately 10 days, contact with cloth reached about 9 hours per day, while wire contact remained below 1.5 hours. The preference persisted during the ensuing observation period. An initial defensive response therefore gave way to selective attachment through repeated experience.

This later acquisition differs from the narrow early interval for untreated chick imprinting. The tactile surrogate preference remained learnable after infancy under these rearing conditions. Developmental timing depends on the behavior and the sensory relationship being learned, rather than a single universal attachment window.

slides.title: Tactile care supports learning of an odor
body: Young rat pups learn preferences for odors paired with tactile stimulation resembling maternal care. Cui and colleagues exposed 6-day-old pups to peppermint odor for 10 minutes while stroking them with a soft brush for alternating 30-second intervals.

The **olfactory bulb** is the brain structure that first processes input from odor-detecting sensory neurons. Its mitral and tufted neurons send processed odor information onward. The investigators measured **cAMP**, cyclic adenosine monophosphate, a chemical messenger inside cells that links stimulation to further signaling.

Paired odor and stroking produced a transient bulb cAMP increase with a rapid decline after training. Odor alone and stroking alone produced different time courses. The temporal relationship between a sensory cue and care-related stimulation therefore changes the biochemical response associated with odor learning.

slides.title: Mitral cells carry learning-related signaling
body: **Mitral cells** are projection neurons of the olfactory bulb, so changes within them can alter the odor information transmitted to other brain regions. cAMP staining identified these cells as a major location of the conditioning-related response.

After effective odor conditioning, cAMP labeling increased in mitral cells as well as in measurements of the whole bulb. The tissue images linked the biochemical change to a neuronal population rather than leaving it as an unidentified signal averaged across all cell types.

The study relates this response to **CREB**, a protein whose phosphorylation can regulate gene expression involved in longer-lasting neuronal changes. The proposed mechanism connects a brief care-associated cAMP signal to modifications that support a later preference for the odor paired with that experience.

slides.title: Adrenergic dose changes cAMP dynamics
body: **Norepinephrine** is a neuromodulator associated with the reinforcing effect of tactile stimulation in neonatal odor learning. The drug **isoproterenol** activates beta-adrenergic receptors, the receptors through which norepinephrine can stimulate cAMP production in bulb neurons.

At 2 mg/kg, isoproterenol paired with odor produced a cAMP increase near the end of the 10-minute training period, followed by a decline 5 minutes later. This dose supports odor-preference learning in the conditioning preparation.

A 6 mg/kg dose produced a larger, more sustained response but was ineffective for the learned preference. Greater messenger accumulation therefore did not correspond to stronger learning. The effective signal included both an increase and its termination, connecting receptor stimulation to a particular temporal pattern of intracellular activity.

slides.title: Odor pairing changes the timing of signaling
body: The effect of a reinforcing drug depended on whether an odor accompanied it. Cui and colleagues compared the same 2 mg/kg isoproterenol dose with and without odor exposure, measuring bulb cAMP at the end of training and shortly afterward.

Odor pairing produced an elevated response at the end of the encounter and a decline 5 minutes later. The drug alone lacked that same rise-and-fall sequence. Pharmacological receptor activation and a sensory cue therefore interacted to shape the signaling time course.

slides.title: PDE4 inhibition enables a low-dose response
body: **Phosphodiesterase 4**, or PDE4, is an enzyme that breaks down cAMP. Inhibiting it changes the balance between messenger production and removal. Cui and colleagues combined the PDE4 inhibitor cilomilast with a low isoproterenol dose.

Isoproterenol at 1 mg/kg was ineffective by itself, but pairing it with 1 mg/kg cilomilast supported odor-preference learning. The combined treatment produced a training-associated cAMP increase followed by a rapid decrease after training.

Messenger degradation is therefore part of the learning-related signaling process rather than merely a passive cleanup step. slides.title: Maternal presence changes odor-shock learning
body: Rat pups aged 12–15 days learned to avoid an odor paired with shock when their mother was absent, but learned to approach that odor when she was present. The same sensory pairing acquired opposite behavioral significance in different social contexts.

Moriceau and Sullivan paired a 30-second peppermint presentation with a 1-second, 0.5 mA shock. The mother was anesthetized during conditioning, preventing active caregiving from explaining the difference. A next-day choice test compared the conditioned odor with familiar bedding.

Age altered this social regulation. At 8 days, pups acquired attraction with or without the mother; at 21–23 days, they acquired aversion in both conditions. Maternal regulation operated during a transitional developmental interval in which **amygdala** circuits supporting threat learning became accessible.

slides.title: A caregiver suppresses stress-hormone signaling
body: **Corticosterone** is a glucocorticoid stress hormone in rats. During odor-shock conditioning, maternal presence reduced the pup’s corticosterone response. The social context therefore changed an internal hormonal signal as well as the later behavioral choice.

Giving corticosterone systemically before conditioning restored odor avoidance despite the mother’s presence. This manipulation connects the maternal reduction in hormone signaling to the switch from aversion to attraction during the transitional age interval.

The hormonal state regulates access to learning-related amygdala activity. A caregiver can alter what is learned about a threatening event by buffering the endocrine response during the encounter. The behavioral effect arises during conditioning rather than requiring the mother to be present during the subsequent choice test.

slides.title: Amygdala recruitment depends on social context
body: The **basolateral and lateral amygdala nuclei** are cell groups involved in the learned significance of sensory cues. Odor-shock pairing without the mother increased metabolic activity in these nuclei, whereas pairing with her present preferentially engaged the olfactory bulb.

The investigators used labeled **2-deoxyglucose**, a glucose-related compound taken up during cellular energy use. This measure localized changes in metabolic activity. Maternal presence changed which learning-related neural structures were recruited during the same conditioning procedure.

Local muscimol, a **GABA-A receptor agonist** that increases inhibitory receptor activity, blocked odor aversion in pups trained without the mother. It spared attraction learned with her present. Amygdala involvement therefore depended on the behavioral significance acquired by the odor, rather than all forms of odor learning requiring that region.

slides.title: Cross-species fostering changes early experience
body: **Cross-fostering** places a newborn with a caregiver other than its biological mother. Kendrick and colleagues reciprocally fostered sheep with goat mothers and goats with sheep mothers, separating the offspring’s inherited species identity from the species of its principal early caregiver.

The fostered young also had social contact with members of their own species. Maternal species was therefore not identical to the only species available during development. Later preference tests offered animals from both species as potential social or mating partners.

Cross-fostered offspring favored partners of their maternal species, especially males. A familiar caregiver relationship influenced which adult animals subsequently attracted social approach and mating behavior, even when other developmental encounters supplied experience with the offspring’s own species.

body: Male goats raised by sheep mothers and male sheep raised by goat mothers strongly preferred females of their foster mother’s species. During adult social-choice tests, cross-fostered males spent about 89% of their time with females of the maternal species.

Mating behavior followed the same species preference. The effect was therefore expressed in both proximity to a social partner and a more specific reproductive action. Preference did not simply follow the male’s inherited species identity.

The males retained this bias after 3 years living exclusively with members of their own species. Early maternal experience established a durable target for adult attraction, while extensive later social exposure failed to redirect that preference under the conditions tested.

slides.title: Cross-fostering changes selected behavioral domains
body: Fostered sheep and goats directed play and grooming preferentially toward animals resembling their maternal species. These affiliative activities involve choosing a partner, so an early caregiver relationship can change whom the developing animal approaches during social interaction.

Other behavior retained the offspring’s own species pattern. Aggression, climbing, feeding and vocalization were not generally transformed into the foster species’ characteristic behavior. Maternal rearing altered partner-directed affiliation more selectively than the animal’s entire behavioral repertoire.

Adult social and sexual preferences extended the early change in partner selection. Cross-fostering therefore separates learned recognition of attractive companions from inherited behavioral organization. An animal can retain species-typical actions while directing some of those actions toward a different species because of early social experience.

slides.title: Social and sexual choices require separate measures
body: Social preference concerns which partner an animal approaches or remains near; sexual preference concerns the target of mating behavior. Kendrick and colleagues measured both in adult sheep and goats, allowing the consequences of maternal rearing to be compared across behavioral systems.

Cross-fostered males strongly preferred the maternal species in both measures. Cross-fostered females retained some social preference but were more flexible in their sexual responses and subsequent changes in partner choice. A single proximity measure would have missed these differences.

The inherited species remained available during rearing, including situations where an opposite-sex twin was reared with its own species. Maternal attachment nevertheless influenced preference. The effect was associated with the principal early caregiver relationship rather than merely the presence of any familiar opposite-sex animal.

slides.title: Female preferences change with later experience
body: Cross-fostered females showed weaker and more reversible maternal-species preferences than cross-fostered males. After 1–2 years of living with their own species, their choices shifted toward those later social partners.

The same rearing manipulation therefore had different persistence in the two sexes. Male preferences remained strongly biased toward the foster mother’s species after 3 years, while female preferences changed over a shorter period of subsequent conspecific contact.

**Conspecifics** are members of the same species. Their availability during later life supplied new social experience rather than changing the animal’s inherited identity. The sex difference concerns the continuing plasticity of partner selection: early attachment could establish a bias that later experience modified more readily in females.

slides.title: Female faces retain caregiver-species significance
body: Sheep and goats also chose between pictures of female faces from the two species. Cross-fostered animals preferred faces resembling their maternal species, linking adult partner selection to visual recognition as well as encounters with living partners.

The investigators recorded both the initial approach and time spent within 1.5 m of a picture during a 120-second test. Male biases were stronger than female biases, matching the broader sex difference in persistence of the rearing effect.

These visual choices identify one sensory route by which an early caregiver can influence later attraction. Familiar species-related facial features retain behavioral significance after development. Recognition of those features can direct approach even when a live partner’s movement and ongoing social interaction are absent.

slides.title: Costumed caregivers supply species-related cues
body: Hand-reared Mississippi sandhill cranes received care from humans wearing gray costumes and using crane-head puppets. The costumes concealed ordinary human appearance, while the puppet guided chicks toward insects and other natural food during supervised foraging.

The rearing program combined these substitutes with crane vocalizations, adult models and access to live adult cranes in adjacent pens. Substitute care therefore preserved several species-related cues rather than asking a single artificial object to replace every parental function.

The behavioral goal was competent foraging with limited attraction to ordinary humans. Caregiving could direct food discovery while its visible form emphasized crane identity. This arrangement applied knowledge of early social learning to preparation for life outside the captive rearing setting.

slides.title: Release exposes juveniles to a natural social setting
body: Parent-reared cranes learned with biological or foster crane parents, whereas hand-reared cranes received costume and puppet care. Both rearing methods were followed by preparation for release into the Mississippi refuge, where survival required natural foraging and avoidance of hazards.

Juveniles were assigned to hand-reared, parent-reared or mixed release groups. The groups stayed together before transport and spent about a month in a refuge acclimation enclosure. Wild cranes visited the release pens, providing contact with the receiving population.

Temporary wing restraints were removed before free release. Radio tracking then followed the birds beyond the controlled enclosure. The transition combined early caregiving history, juvenile social companions and experience of the release environment, all of which could influence subsequent behavior in the wild.

slides.title: Survival tests the consequences of rearing
body: Estimated survival during the first year after release was about 80% across the crane rearing treatments. Hand-reared birds survived at least as well as parent-reared birds under the costume-rearing and release procedures used by Ellis and colleagues.

The comparison evaluated an outcome beyond attachment or performance in a captive test. Free-ranging birds had to find food, move through habitat and respond to predators. Successful hand rearing therefore required development of behavior compatible with those natural demands.

Radio transmitters could fail before a bird died, and some cranes reappeared more than 2 years after last detection. The investigators distinguished disappearance from confirmed mortality when estimating survival. This distinction changes how field outcomes are interpreted: loss of a signal is not equivalent to loss of the animal.

slides.title: Mixed cohorts improve post-release survival
body: Cranes released in mixed hand-reared and parent-reared cohorts survived better than birds released in unmixed cohorts. Parent-reared birds benefited particularly strongly from mixed groups, connecting the social composition of release to a later field outcome.

The authors proposed a hypothesis that the groups combined different behavioral strengths. Parent-reared cranes could contribute natural foraging skills, whereas costume-reared birds might be more wary of ordinary humans because their caregivers had concealed human appearance.

These proposed mechanisms concern social learning and responses to potential danger after release. The measured result is the survival advantage of mixed cohorts. A substitute-care program can therefore include later opportunities for learning from peers with different early experience, rather than depending entirely on the original surrogate caregiver.

items.text: Early social experience gives particular visual or olfactory cues selective control over approach, following and attachment behavior.
Local T4-to-T3 conversion promotes chick imprinting, and early T3 exposure primes later learning beyond the usual sensitive period.
T3 acts effectively in IMM, an intact IMHA is required downstream, and post-training IMHA lesions disrupt later preference expression.
Cloth contact attracts rhesus infants independently of milk, while early robot exposure changes quail coordination and separation distress.
Transient olfactory-bulb cAMP accompanies effective neonatal odor conditioning; maternal corticosterone buffering changes amygdala-dependent threat learning.
Cross-fostering alters partner preferences with sex-dependent persistence, and mixed crane release cohorts improve survival after substitute care.
